title: Speed to lead: why the first call back wins | Blog
summary: Speed to lead is how fast you reach a new lead. See what the research says, what a good response time looks like, and how AI agents reach leads in seconds.
body_markdown:
Leads reach out on their own schedule. Many homeowners fill out quote requests in the late evening or early morning, but most sales teams won’t see it until office hours. That delay holds a lot more significance than you might think. Speed to lead measures the gap between a lead and a call back, and the brand that closes it first is often the one that gets the deal.


## What is speed to lead?


Speed to lead is how long it takes a new lead to reach a real conversation with your brand. The clock starts when the lead arrives, by form, quote request, text or call, and stops when they reach a live rep or an AI agent. An auto-reply or voicemail doesn’t count.


## Why does speed to lead matter?


The best-known research on this dates to 2007, but the industry still treats it as a foundational study. MIT’s James Oldroyd and[InsideSales.com](http://insidesales.com/) studied more than 15,000 web-form leads and over 100,000 call attempts across six companies. The odds of qualifying a lead fell 21 times between a call at 5 minutes and a call at 30 minutes, and dropped more than 6 times within the first hour. The study measured qualification rather than closed sales, and it looked at web forms rather than texts or inbound calls. We read it as a direction. For a consumer brand, that direction says to count response time in minutes, rather than hours.


## What is a good speed-to-lead time?


For a consumer brand, a good speed-to-lead time is seconds to a few minutes. The 2007 study used 5 minutes as its fastest window. AI agents can beat that because they don’t have to finish another call first. The lead’s clock keeps running at 9pm, on weekends and through a holiday rush: an agent’s response time stays consistent no matter what.


## Which businesses feel speed to lead most?


Speed to lead matters most for consumer brands that sell over the phone, which is who we build for. A homeowner asks for a window quote, a shopper calls about an order, an applicant starts a loan application. Each one is waiting on a reply, and each often reach out long after your office has closed.


## Why do leads end up waiting?


Leads wait when your employees are busy with something else. With many human reps juggling multiple responsibilities and limited resources, this makes a lot of sense. They can only talk to one customer at a time, after all. After hours, no one is there to answer. At Renewal by Andersen, the overnight overflow went to a third-party call center, and unfortunately that meant poor lead quality and misrouted leads.


The gap is widest in two moments. Who picks up when a lead arrives at 9pm, after the last shift has gone home? And who calls back when several leads land in the same busy hour? Either way, your leads are left waiting.


## How can you shorten your speed to lead?


Teams usually have three levers. The first is more coverage: staffing more people across more hours, which works until volume spikes or the evening shift is the thin one. The second is smarter routing, sending each new lead to whoever is free first rather than whoever owns the account, which trims the wait. The third is putting an AI agent on the first response, so every lead gets an answer right away and a rep steps in when the conversation calls for one.


## How does an AI agent respond in seconds, on the channel the lead chose?


Leads come in through ads, quote forms, click-to-call buttons and aggregator lists. Simple responds on whichever channel they used, across phone, text, email and web, and keeps one memory of the conversation so no one has to repeat themselves. A[sales conversation](https://www.usesimple.ai/use-cases/sales) with Simple moves through four stages.


1.


**The lead arrives.** A form, a quote request or a text comes in, and Simple starts the conversation within seconds (or the timing you decide on).


2.


**Simple reaches them on their channel.** A lead who called gets a call, and a lead who texted gets a text. If there’s no answer, Simple tries another channel and builds on what the lead already shared.


3.


**The follow-up continues.** If the lead can’t talk, Simple works out a better time and calls or texts back then, remembering the first conversation.


4.


**A rep steps in when it matters.** Your reps see who the lead is, what they asked and what Simple has already done, so they can take over without starting from scratch and hand back when they’re done.


## How does speed to lead connect marketing to sales?


Marketing pays to get a lead’s attention, and speed to lead decides what happens in the minutes after it works. Leads don’t always stay on one channel, either. Someone might click an ad, text a question that evening and call the next day, but you always want them to feel they’re speaking to the same person. Simple keeps one memory of the conversation across phone, text, email and web, so each response picks up where the last one left off.


## What should you measure?


Start with time to first contact, measured from the moment a lead arrives to the first real conversation and broken out by lead source and by hour of day. That breakdown will show you which sources get answered fastest, which hours get answered slowest, and whether leads convert differently once they’re reached sooner. From there, follow what happens next: contact rate, appointments set, conversion and revenue per lead. Revenue per lead matters most, because it shows whether a faster response is turning into more sales.


## How do you start with speed to lead?


Pick one lead source, such as web quote requests or an aggregator list, and run Simple on it alongside your current process. Before it starts, agree on what counts as the first real conversation and when the clock starts, so both sides are measured the same way. Then compare time to first contact, appointments set and revenue per lead against the same source before, and run it long enough to cover evenings and weekends, when leads are most likely to be left waiting. Once the first response is fast, the next question is what happens to leads who don’t answer or aren’t ready yet.


## The takeaway


Speed to lead comes down to being the first brand a new lead talks to, which for phone, text and web leads means answering in seconds, at any hour, on the channel they used.
